what_it_is: The plantar fascia is a thick band of tissue running along the bottom of your foot from the heel bone to the front of the foot. It supports your arch and helps with push-off as you walk. Plantar fasciitis is irritation of this band near its attachment on the inner part of the heel. The name suggests inflammation, but the APTA heel pain guideline describes a spectrum that includes both inflammatory and degenerative changes.

The American Physical Therapy Association estimates it affects as many as 2 million Americans each year and about 10% of people over their lifetimes. It is most common between ages 40 and 60. Runners, people carrying extra weight, and those who stand on hard surfaces for much of the day, such as teachers, factory workers and healthcare staff, are especially prone, according to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons.
symptoms: Sharp or stabbing pain on the bottom of the heel
Pain with the first steps out of bed in the morning
Pain that returns after sitting or resting, then eases as you walk
Heel pain after long periods of standing or activity
Pain climbing stairs or walking barefoot
causes: A sudden increase in walking, running or standing
Long hours standing on hard surfaces

how_therapy_helps.intro: Physical therapy has a deep evidence base for heel pain, and the American Physical Therapy Association notes that most cases improve with conservative treatment and surgery is rarely needed. The 2023 APTA heel pain clinical practice guideline gives its strongest grade to manual therapy, plantar fascia and calf stretching, foot taping, and night splints for people whose pain is worst with the first step in the morning. It also recommends resistance training for the foot and ankle muscles.
methods: Specific stretches for the fascia and the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles, recommended in the APTA guideline for short- and long-term pain reduction.
Joint and soft tissue techniques for the foot, ankle and calf to improve mobility and ease pain.
Rigid or elastic taping to support the arch and offload the fascia, used together with other treatment.
Resistance exercise for the small muscles of the foot along with the ankle and calf, progressed as pain allows.
For persistent first-step pain, the guideline supports a 1 to 3 month program of night splints that keep the foot in a gentle stretch while you sleep.
Help choosing supportive shoes and, when useful, arch supports. The guideline advises using orthoses alongside other treatment rather than on their own.

first_visit: Your therapist will ask when the heel pain started, what changed in your activity or footwear, and how the first steps of the day feel. The exam includes pressing along the heel and arch to locate tenderness, measuring ankle and big toe flexibility, checking calf and foot strength, and watching you walk. Your therapist will also screen for other causes of heel pain, such as nerve irritation or a heel stress fracture.
recovery: Plantar fasciitis tends to improve gradually. The APTA guideline notes that many people have had symptoms for more than a year before they seek treatment. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, more than 90% of people with plantar fasciitis improve within 10 months of nonsurgical treatment, and surgery is generally considered only after 12 months of consistent nonsurgical care without improvement. Your progress depends on how long symptoms have been present, your activity demands, and how consistently the home program is done.
self_care: Stretch your calves and the bottom of your foot several times a day, including before your first steps in the morning.
Wear supportive shoes with a low heel and cushioned sole, and avoid walking barefoot on hard floors.
Rest and raise your heel when you can, and ice it after activity for short sessions.
Cut back temporarily on running, jumping or long periods of standing, then build back gradually.
Replace athletic shoes once the cushioning wears out.
see_a_doctor: Severe heel pain after an injury
A foot or ankle that has changed shape or sits at an odd angle
Heel pain that is severe or stopping you from doing normal activities
Pain that has not improved after 2 weeks of home care
Heel pain that began after a sharp jump in running or impact activity and hurts even at rest, which can point to a stress fracture

faqs.q: Why does plantar fasciitis hurt most in the morning?
faqs.a: The APTA heel pain guideline describes plantar fasciitis pain as most noticeable with the first weight-bearing steps in the morning or after a period of rest. Overnight, the foot and calf rest in a relaxed, shortened position, and the first steps suddenly stretch and load the fascia. That is also why night splints, which hold a gentle stretch during sleep, help some people with morning pain.

faqs.q: Do night splints work for plantar fasciitis?
faqs.a: For people who consistently have pain with the first step in the morning, the 2023 APTA clinical practice guideline gives a strong recommendation for a 1 to 3 month program of night splints. The splint keeps the ankle and toes in a mild stretch overnight. They are typically one part of a broader plan that also includes stretching, strengthening and footwear changes.

faqs.q: Is a heel spur the same as plantar fasciitis?
faqs.a: No. A heel spur is a bony growth on the heel bone, while plantar fasciitis involves the band of tissue along the bottom of the foot. The APTA heel pain guideline lists heel spur syndrome as a separate possible cause of plantar heel pain, alongside fat pad problems, nerve irritation and stress fractures. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, most people with heel spurs have no heel pain, and spurs are not the cause of plantar fasciitis pain.

faqs.q: Do I need custom orthotics for plantar fasciitis?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. The 2023 APTA guideline recommends against using orthoses, prefabricated or custom, as the only treatment, and supports them when combined with stretching, strengthening and other care. Supportive shoes and an over-the-counter arch support are often a reasonable starting point. Your therapist can help you decide whether a more specialized option is worth the cost.

faqs.q: Can I keep running with plantar fasciitis?
faqs.a: Many runners can keep some running while they recover, but volume, speed and hills usually need to come down for a while. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons lists rest and activity modification as first-line treatment, and the American Physical Therapy Association recommends increasing activity gradually. Cross-training such as cycling or swimming can help you keep your fitness in the meantime.

The guideline describes the benefit as short-term improvement in pain and function. A therapist can teach you or a family member how to apply it at home.

notes_for_reviewer: ICD-10 M72.2 verified on icd10data.com; it is a non-billable parent titled 'Plantar fascial fibromatosis' with plantar fasciitis listed as an approximate synonym. Billable children are M72.20 to M72.22. Confirm the clinic's preferred code.
The 2023 JOSPT guideline also gives strong grades to dry needling and low-level laser therapy; both were left out because the clinic does not list them.
FAQ on morning pain includes a plain-language mechanism (foot rests in a shortened position overnight) that is not quoted from a source.
The stress fracture red flag is clinical framing built on the guideline's differential diagnosis list; the 'hurts even at rest' wording is not quoted from a source.

Fact-check: grades confirmed in the 2023 CPG summary. Manual therapy, stretching, taping and night splints are grade A; foot and ankle resistance training is grade B; orthoses alone grade B against, combined grade C. Intro now reflects this.
